addition noun

something added

also an addition, a new addition, extension, add-on, supplement, supplementary

classical

Cic. Off. 1.138: accessiōnem adjūnxit aedibus
Cic. Lael. 11: paucōrum annōrum accessiō

accessiō, accessiōnis f.

noun, third declension · Declension on Wiktionary

an addition; something added on, an extension

From accēdere, to come to, be added: what is added is said to accēdere, as in accēdit quod, there is also the fact that (see further). Lewis & Short: “the thing added, the addition”.

Other words

  • additāmentum, additāmentī n. — an addition, something tacked on

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Cic. Sest. 68: Ligus iste nescio quī, additāmentum inimīcōrum meōrum; Sen. Ep. 17.6 (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

    Rare: once in Cicero, of a nobody who merely swells the ranks of his enemies; then Seneca (Lewis & Short).

  • adjectiō, adjectiōnis f. — the adding of something, an addition

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Liv. 1.30.6: Rōmānam rem nūper etiam adjectiōne populī Albānī auctam · Declension on Wiktionary

  • supplēmentum, supplēmentī n. — what fills up or completes; reinforcements

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 3.3.1: supplēmentum legiōnibus scrībere (Lewis & Short); Col. 7.6.7 (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

    Classically a military word, the troops enrolled to bring units up to strength (Cic., Caes., Liv.); of anything that makes a thing whole only after Augustus (Col., Vell.). The verb is supplēre, fill up, make up what is lacking.

Examples

  • Hanc Scaurus dēmōlītus accessiōnem adjūnxit aedibus.

    Scaurus pulled it down and added it to his own house as an extension.Cic. Off. 1.138

  • Quid igitur hunc paucōrum annōrum accessiō juvāre potuisset?

    So what good could the addition of a few years have done him?Cic. Lael. 11

See also further, add, increase.
